senses: On Haiti, the kapok tree, Ceiba pentandra.
examples: The mapou belongs to Legba, the master of the crossroads, one of the most important gods in the pantheon, Apollo to Ogoun's Ares.
It was calm and surprisingly cool in the mapou grove.

senses: To make or conform to a virtual reality.
Having the qualities of or relating to a badger.
examples: A meline musteloid carnivorous mammal, usually burrowing, nocturnal, and having a flat stout body, short legs with long-clawed toes, and a long snout.

senses: A corporation or body of magistrates in cities and towns in Spain, corresponding to mayor and aldermen.
Synonym of dialectal (“of or pertaining to a dialect”).
ety: From Latin dialecticus + -al. By surface analysis, dialectic + -al or dialect + -ical.

senses: The tip of the toe.
ety: From Middle English tipto, typto; equivalent to tip + toe. Compare fingertip.

senses: Goatlike: goatish; goaty.
ety: Borrowed from Latin caprīnus. The taxonomic sense is a semantic loan from translingual Caprinae.

senses: To besiege; to surround with troops.
To vex, harass, or beset.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch belegeren and/or Middle Low German belēgeren; equivalent to be- + lair. Compare also German belagern, Danish belejre. The English spelling was perhaps influenced by unrelated league.

senses: What if, lest (something problematic or unanticipated happens)
Suddenly and unexpectedly.
A laid-back subgenre of trap music.
ety: From "Plug!", earlier "Plugs!", the producer tag used by the members of BeatPluggz collective, who recorded the vocals for the tag.

senses: Examination of the eye with an ophthalmoscope.
The design, construction and use of ophthalmoscopes.
examples: A complete lenticular cataract, be it hard or soft, becomes an object of ophthalmoscopy only in so far, as we can convince ourselves by the oblique illumination that there are no clear unopaque portions of the lens left.

senses: Sensationalized; presented with grand claims.
examples: Waitress: There's a man over there who says he's waiting for you. Niles: Ah. No doubt the much ballyhooed Bob.
Behind the scenes, the system had quietly punched a neat loophole into the ballyhooed reform.

senses: Geographical data.
examples: Statistical quality control as applied to industrial output is a method that can also be used for the control of geodata.

senses: The distance by which one wave is behind another.
The act of diminishing the rate of speed.
The extent to which anything is retarded; the result of any retarding or delay; mental, social, or physical slowness.
That which retards; an obstacle; an obstruction.
A suspension which resolves upwards.
A device for removing the moisture content from air
Someone who is into adventurism.
A politician involved in adventurism.
That leads to apoptosis
A wandering or roving around, especially in search of chivalrous adventure.
ety: From errant + -ry, from Middle English erraunt. See further etymology at errant.

senses: A person who mends.
Shaped like the Greek letter lambda
ety: Borrowed from French lambdoïde, from the New Latin lambdoīdēs, from the Ancient Greek λαβδοειδής (labdoeidḗs).

senses: An expert in sexology.
examples: To sum up: taking money with your clothes on, sexpert. With your clothes off, not. So basically sexperts are reporters about sex, rather than sex professionals. Or something.

senses: A metric form of verse using two rhymes, usually fourteen 8- to 10-syllable lines in three stanzas, with the first lines of the first stanza returning as refrain of the next two.
The verse form rondeau.
A rondelle, (small) circular object.
A long thin medieval dagger with a circular guard and a circular pommel (hence the name).
A small round tower erected at the foot of a bastion.
ety: From Middle English rondel, from Old French rondel, a diminutive of ronde, the feminine of ront, reont (“round (in shape)”), from Latin rotundus (“round, circular; spherical”), related to rota (“wheel”).

senses: A device for routing electrical signals by means of a number of jacks.
examples: U.S. Navy SOUND-POWERED TELEPHONE TALKERS' MANUAL What precaution should you take in unplugging a cable from a jackbox?
Each electrode's wire will be plugged in a jackbox (Fig. 2.9). Many devices often surround the ICU beds; therefore, a small jackbox that can be placed near the patient's head is recommended.

senses: Preventing or treating diarrhea.
Synonym of amin (“arbitrator in the pargana”).
ety: From Hindi मुंसिफ़ (munsif), from Arabic مُنْصِف (munṣif).

senses: Capable of making a poofing sound.
ety: Probably a blend of poof + puffy.

senses: Matricaria chamomilla, German chamomile or Hungarian chamomile, with fragrant flowers used for tea, and as an herbal remedy.
Chamaemelum nobile (formerly Anthemis nobilis), English chamomile or Roman chamomile, a ground cover with fragrant foliage.
Any of several other similar plants. (See below)
ety: From Middle English camamille, first attested 1265, from Old French camomille, from Late Latin camomilla, from Latin chamaemelon, from Ancient Greek χαμαίμηλον (khamaímēlon, literally “earth-apple”), from χαμαί (khamaí, “on the ground”) + μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”). So called because of the apple-like scent of the plant.

senses: A social and political philosophy that advocates an equitable distribution of land.
An untanned leather, often dyed green; originally made from horse skin, today mostly made from the skin of a shark or ray.
ety: First use appears c. 1677, an Anglicized form of chagrin, from French chagrin, from Ottoman Turkish صاغری (modern Turkish sağrı). However, the etymology of French chagrin is complex and disputed, and likely of Germanic origin. Whether there was any influence between an existing French word of Germanic origin and a Turkish loan is unclear.

senses: an oxidizing agent
German culture or civilization, especially seen as authoritarian or racist during the period of world wars (1914-18 and 1939-45)
ety: Borrowed from German Kultur, from Latin cultūra; doublet of culture.

senses: The state of being malignant or diseased.
A malignant cancer; specifically, any neoplasm that is invasive or otherwise not benign.
That which is malign; evil, depravity, malevolence.
ety: From malignant + -cy or malign + -ancy or Latin malignantia.

senses: A wind blowing from the south.
The branch of medicine dealing with diseases of the lungs and respiratory tract.
Characteristic of lovers.
The number or expression written above the line in a fraction (such as 1 in ½).
An enumerator; someone who counts.
ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin numerātor.

senses: A Nordic poet of the Viking Age.
ety: From Old Norse skald. Doublet of scold.

senses: The business entity in which an investment is made.
examples: Many of his investee companies have been found to encourage fraud, regulators have said.
In minority active investments, an investor acquires common shares of an investee with the intent of exerting significant influence over the investee's activities.

senses: Resembling a hydatid.
To supinate.
To lie back into a supine position.
ety: From Latin resupino, where the re- prefix occurs in its "back or backward" sense, not its "again" sense.
